unit.name: Multi-agent workflow patterns and smart-home example
unit.description: Introduces why multi-agent workflows are useful, especially for parallelism, reuse, fault isolation, and hierarchical orchestration, illustrated through a smart-home automation exercise.
unit.summary: The final technical section asks why multi-agent workflows are needed when a single workflow already has multiple steps, model calls, and tools [ts=5665s]. The main answer is parallelism: multi-agent systems are useful when independent specialized tasks should run in parallel, with the additional advantage that agents can be reused across teams or products [ts=5692s]. Students design smart-home agents for biometrics/location, temperature, energy, security, groceries, and orchestration [ts=5743s]. The instructor identifies a hierarchical pattern where the user mainly talks to an orchestrator, which delegates to specialized agents [ts=5863s]. The slide list includes climate control, lighting, security, energy management, entertainment, notification, and orchestrator agents [ts=6081s]. The segment closes with organization patterns such as flat and hierarchical systems, and advantages such as easier debugging and parallelization [ts=6101s].

key_points.text: Multi-agent workflows are most useful when parts of the task can run in parallel.
Reusable specialized agents can serve multiple teams or workflows within a company.
A smart-home system can be decomposed into specialized agents such as biometric/location tracking, temperature, and energy agents.
An orchestrator agent can serve as the main user communication point and delegate to other agents.
Smart-home agents can include climate control, lighting, security, energy management, entertainment, notifications, and orchestration.
Multi-agent systems may be organized as flat or hierarchical interaction patterns.
Multi-agent workflows can improve debugging and parallelization compared with a monolithic single agent.
